item.title: “Monks, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a monk delights in those forms,…
item.description:
“Monks, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a monk delights in those forms, praises them, and dwells with lust for them — then, monks, this is called a monk who has gone into Māra’s domain, who has come under Māra’s control. Māra’s net has surrounded him. Bound by Māra, he is subject to the Evil One’s will … Monks, there are phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable … enticing. If a monk delights in those phenomena, praises them, and dwells with lust for them — then, monks, this is called a monk who has gone into Māra’s domain, who has come under Māra’s control. Māra’s net has surrounded him. Bound by Māra, he is subject to the Evil One’s will.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.114

item.title: Sitting down to one side, the Venerable Rādha said to the Blessed One: “Good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma…
item.description:
Sitting down to one side, the Venerable Rādha said to the Blessed One: “Good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief. Having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I will dwell alone, secluded, heedful, ardent, and resolute.” - “Rādha, whatever is impermanent — there you should abandon your desire. And what, Rādha, is impermanent? The eye, Rādha, is impermanent — there you should abandon your desire. Forms are impermanent … Eye-consciousness … Eye-contact … Whatever feeling arises dependent on eye-contact — pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant — that feeling is impermanent. There you should abandon your desire. The ear … The nose … The tongue … The body … The mind is impermanent — there you should abandon your desire. Phenomena … Mind-consciousness … Mind-contact … Whatever feeling arises dependent on mind-contact — pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant — that feeling is impermanent. There you should abandon your desire. Whatever is impermanent, Rādha — there you should abandon your desire.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.76
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief. Having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I will dwell…
item.description:
“Good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief. Having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I will dwell alone, secluded, heedful, ardent, and resolute.” - “Koṭṭhita, whatever is suffering — there you should abandon your desire. And what, Koṭṭhita, is suffering? The eye is suffering — there you should abandon your desire. Forms are suffering — there you should abandon your desire. Eye-consciousness is suffering — there you should abandon your desire. Eye-contact is suffering — there you should abandon your desire. Whatever feeling arises dependent on eye-contact — pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant — that feeling is suffering. There you should abandon your desire.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.163

item.title: “Udāyi, there are these five strands of sensual pleasure. What five? Forms cognizable by the eye—desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. Sounds cognizable…
item.description:
“Udāyi, there are these five strands of sensual pleasure. What five? Forms cognizable by the eye—desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. Sounds cognizable by the ear … Odors cognizable by the nose … Tastes cognizable by the tongue … Tangibles cognizable by the body—desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. These, Udāyi, are the five strands of sensual pleasure. Whatever pleasure or joy arises in dependence on these five strands of sensual pleasure, that is called sensual pleasure, defiled pleasure, worldling’s pleasure, ignoble pleasure. I say that such pleasure should not be pursued, should not be developed, should not be cultivated, should be feared.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 66 – Laṭukikopamasutta

item.title: “Monks, these six sense bases — well-guarded, well-protected, well-guarded, well-restrained — bring happiness. What six? The eye sense base, monks — well-guarded, well-protected, well-guarded, well-restrained…
item.description:
“Monks, these six sense bases — well-guarded, well-protected, well-guarded, well-restrained — bring happiness. What six? The eye sense base, monks — well-guarded, well-protected, well-guarded, well-restrained — brings happiness. The ear … The nose … The tongue … The body … The mind sense base, monks — well-guarded, well-protected, well-guarded, well-restrained — brings happiness. These six sense bases, monks — well-guarded, well-protected, well-guarded, well-restrained — bring happiness.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.94

item.title: “Form, monks, is impermanent. Whatever cause and condition for the arising of form — that too is impermanent. Form that has arisen from the impermanent,…
item.description:
“Form, monks, is impermanent. Whatever cause and condition for the arising of form — that too is impermanent. Form that has arisen from the impermanent, monks, how could it be permanent? Feeling, monks, is impermanent … Perception … Formations … Consciousness is impermanent. Whatever cause and condition for the arising of consciousness — that too is impermanent. Consciousness that has arisen from the impermanent, monks, how could it be permanent? Seeing thus, monks, a well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form … disenchanted with feeling … disenchanted with perception … disenchanted with formations … disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate … He knows: ‘… there is no more of this state of being.’”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.18
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, suppose the Ganges river carries along a great pile of foam. A person with good eyesight would look at it, reflect, and examine it.…
item.description:
“Monks, suppose the Ganges river carries along a great pile of foam. A person with good eyesight would look at it, reflect, and examine it. Looking, reflecting, examining, the foam would appear empty, hollow, insubstantial. For what substance could there be in a pile of foam? So too, monks, whatever form there is, past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near — a monk sees form, reflects, examines it. Seeing, reflecting, examining, form appears empty, hollow, insubstantial. For what substance could there be in form?”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.95
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Good sirs, what is suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, sickness is suffering, death is suffering, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, despair are suffering, not…
item.description:
“Good sirs, what is suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, sickness is suffering, death is suffering, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, despair are suffering, not getting what one wants is suffering; in short, the five clinging-aggregates are suffering. This, good sirs, is called suffering. Good sirs, what is the origin of suffering? It is craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, delighting here and there; that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, craving for non-existence. This, good sirs, is called the origin of suffering.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 9 – Sammādiṭṭhisutta

item.title: “Once, monks, a hawk suddenly swooped down and seized a quail. Then, monks, the quail, while being carried off by the hawk, lamented: ‘This is…
item.description:
“Once, monks, a hawk suddenly swooped down and seized a quail. Then, monks, the quail, while being carried off by the hawk, lamented: ‘This is my misfortune! This is my lack of merit! For I wandered outside my own proper range, into the domain of others. If I had kept to my own proper range, my ancestral territory, this hawk would not have been a match for me in battle.’ - ‘What, quail, is your own proper range, your ancestral territory?’ - ‘A field plowed with a plow.’ Then, monks, the hawk, not boasting of its own strength, not pressing its own strength, released the quail and said: ‘Go, quail. Even after going there, I will not let you go.’ Then, monks, the quail went to a field plowed with a plow, climbed onto a large clod of earth, stood on it, and said to the hawk: ‘Come at me, hawk! Come at me, hawk!’ Then the hawk, boasting of its own strength, pressing its own strength, folding both wings, suddenly swooped down on the quail. When the quail knew: ‘This hawk is swooping down hard on me,’ it hid behind that clod of earth. Then, monks, the hawk shattered its own breast. So too, monks, for one who wanders outside his own proper range, into the domain of others. Therefore, monks, do not wander outside your own proper range, into the domain of others. For one who wanders outside his proper range, into the domain of others, Māra gains an opportunity, Māra gains an object.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 47.6

item.title: “Monks, if a monk lives without ardor in his practice, though he may wish: ‘May my mind be liberated from the defilements without clinging,’ yet…
item.description:
“Monks, if a monk lives without ardor in his practice, though he may wish: ‘May my mind be liberated from the defilements without clinging,’ yet his mind is not liberated from the defilements without clinging. Why is that? It is because he has not developed. Not developed what? He has not developed the four foundations of mindfulness. He has not developed the four right efforts. He has not developed the four bases of spiritual power. He has not developed the five faculties. He has not developed the five powers. He has not developed the seven factors of enlightenment. He has not developed the Noble Eightfold Path.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.101
